title: Seven sample courses, and courses with labs, code and languages
lede: Four more sample courses to explore, and fixes from check-ups of a ratios unit, a Spanish course and a statistics course taught with R. Two of them were plain bugs that would have broken a real class.

sections.heading: Seven sample courses, by stage
sections.body: The sample chooser now groups courses by stage, with four new ones. Like the first three, each was written by Folio from a teacher’s brief, then read lesson by lesson and corrected.
bullets: The water cycle, grade 5: five lessons built from a teacher’s own planning notes, with supports for struggling readers and a Spanish-speaking newcomer in every lesson.
Ratios and rates, grade 6: eight lessons with no homework, assessed by two in-class quizzes and a unit test with a full mark scheme.
Stoichiometry, grade 10: ten lessons with two labs, four problem sets with answer keys, and a unit test.
Reconstruction, 1865–1877, grade 11: eight lessons on named primary sources, a Socratic seminar and a document-based essay.

image.alt: The sample chooser with seven courses under elementary, middle, high school and university

sections.heading: A lab unit you could run
sections.body: The chemistry sample shows what the lab fixes add up to: quantities for a whole class, goggles, gloves and ventilation, a warning about the heat a reaction gives off, what to do for a splash in the eye, and how to dispose of the waste. The copper left to dry in one lesson is weighed in the next, and every problem set has new problems and an answer key.

image.alt: A chemistry lab lesson: predicting the limiting reactant before reacting aluminum with copper chloride

sections.heading: History from the documents
sections.body: The Reconstruction sample names every source students read, down to the passage, and tells you to prepare copies. Its essay lists the documents the unit actually used, its seminar has scoring a whole class can reach, and every exit ticket has its question and a simple score. Painful material comes with guidance: slurs are never read aloud, and no one plays a victim or an attacker.

image.alt: The map of the Reconstruction unit: eight lessons with plans, slides, study guides, quizzes and the essay

sections.heading: Code stays code
sections.body: Folio tidies quotation marks into curly ones. It was doing that inside code too, so every line of R with text in it failed when a student pasted it. Code is now left exactly as written. In our statistics course, 607 pieces of code, none changed.

sections.heading: “A lecture and a computer lab” is two meetings
sections.body: A brief that asked for “a 75-minute lecture and a 50-minute computer lab” each week got lectures only: the lab was missed because of the word “computer” in between. Folio now reads it as two meetings and plans both.

compare.before: Each week: one 75-minute lecture, with students somehow at computers.
compare.after: Each week: a 75-minute lecture and a 50-minute lab, each with its own plan.

sections.heading: A language course speaks the language
sections.body: Discussion prompts in a Spanish course were English debates about Spanish. They now get students using the language at their level. A lesson that teaches many words can also list all of them, not just eight.

compare.before: “A friend says, ‘Using usted is old-fashioned. We should just use tú with everyone.’ Do you agree?”
compare.after: “Imagina que tu compañero te pregunta: ¿Cómo estás? Hoy no te sientes ni bien ni mal. ¿Dices Regular o Bien?”

sections.heading: Also in this release
bullets: The class policies in your syllabus (late work, integrity, accommodations) are carried into the course.
A quiz or test has points for each question, enough time, and nothing left on the board that answers it.
A lesson’s graded quiz is the lesson’s own quiz, not a second set of questions.
The close of a lesson tells students what is coming next, including a quiz, and what to read.
A project due weeks after it is set asks for what the lessons up to then teach.
A weekly problem set repeats none of the last one’s problems.

title: A second read that changes the plan, and homework that is new work
lede: We wrote six more courses overnight, from grade 3 fractions to a college psychology course built from a syllabus, and had each one read lesson by lesson the way its teacher would. These are the fixes that came out of it.

sections.heading: When the second read finds a problem, the plan is rewritten
sections.body: Every lesson plan gets a second read before anything is built on it. Small fixes were made on the spot, but anything bigger used to be left as a note for you, while the slides, quiz and study guide were built on the flawed plan and repeated it. Now a plan left with notes is written once more, told what the read found, and read again. Whichever version comes out cleaner is kept. In our chemistry and history courses, the notes left for the teacher went from four each to none.

image.alt: Before, a review note stayed on an unchanged plan. Now the plan is rewritten with the note and read again

sections.heading: Homework is new work, not the class examples again
sections.body: Problem sets and quiz questions were being told to use the plan’s examples, so graded homework repeated what the class had just worked through together, with the answers already on the board. Now they keep the lesson’s methods and facts but give students new problems.

compare.before: In class: “6.0 mol H₂ makes how many mol NH₃?” For homework: “find the moles of NH₃ made from 6.0 mol H₂.”
compare.after: For homework: “For 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, write the mole ratio of Mg to MgO. Use it to find the moles of MgO made from 3.60 mol Mg.”

image.alt: A grade 10 chemistry problem set on mole ratios with new problems

sections.heading: Steps that build toward the big piece
sections.body: When several lessons set a step toward an essay or a paper, or a problem set every few days, each used to be written on its own. One course set the same step three lessons running. Now they are written in order, each knowing what the ones before asked, so steps build on each other and recurring work keeps one length and format. Homework also follows the rhythm you ask for: “twice a week” is twice a week, not every lesson.

image.alt: Before: the same step set three times. Now: an evidence log, a working claim, connecting evidence, then the essay

sections.heading: Tests have a lesson, questions, answers and points
sections.body: A unit test worth half the grade used to be only “previewed” in the last lesson. Now graded work that happens in class is given a lesson when the course is outlined, and a lesson with a test writes its questions, answer key and points out in full, asks about new cases, and keeps them out of that lesson’s study guide and quiz. The same goes for an exit ticket: its question and expected answer are in the plan. (A printable test paper as its own material is still to come.)

image.alt: The last lesson of a chemistry unit, now a 55-minute unit test with its rules and timing

sections.heading: Care with hard material, and with what students handle
sections.body: Plans now say how to handle painful content, and never ask students to play the people who suffered or inflicted it. Lab plans cover what a careful teacher would: protective gear, ventilation, the heat a reaction gives off, and disposal.

compare.before: “You are a returning Confederate soldier or a newly freed person in Georgia. What is the first problem you must solve?”
compare.after: “Violence is the content. Warn students before you begin, give plain facts without graphic detail, and let anyone step out quietly. Never assign roles of victims or attackers.”

sections.heading: Lessons hand over to each other
sections.body: A plan now knows what homework its own lesson sets and sets it before students leave; the next lesson collects or uses it. It knows what students should read before the next lesson and tells them. Later lessons see how earlier ones set things up, down to the teacher notes, and finish what was left for them, like a lab result waiting to be measured. Work that runs over several days is started early enough when the course is outlined.
bullets: Texts students read are named exactly, down to the passage, with a note to prepare copies; never just “an excerpt”.
A final essay asks only for what the course really gave students.
A paper for the whole course takes its topic from your brief, not from the lesson that happens to set it.
Slides show the items students work from, and hold back the answers until the reveal.
University courses say “instructor”, and keep any routine your syllabus asks for.

title: Sample courses, and courses that hold together
lede: Folio’s first numbered release. Three new sample courses to explore, and a round of improvements to how every course is written, found by building those samples to the standard of a teacher who has to teach them tomorrow.

sections.heading: Three sample courses, one for each stage
sections.body: “Or open a sample course” now lets you choose. Each one was written by Folio from a teacher’s brief, the same way your courses are, then read lesson by lesson and polished. Open one, change anything, export it: it is your own copy.
bullets: Elementary: plant and animal life cycles, a ten-lesson grade 2 science unit with a bean garden students watch grow.
Middle school: writing argumentative essays, a fifteen-lesson grade 8 unit built on two opinion articles about later school start times.
University: introduction to ethics, a fourteen-week semester with a lecture and a seminar every week.

image.alt: The sample chooser: elementary school, middle school and university

sections.heading: A full course at a glance
sections.body: Each sample is the size a teacher there would plan: a unit for school, a whole semester for university, with every lesson’s plan, slides, study guide, quiz, assignment, rubric, discussion questions and answers to students’ questions.

image.alt: The map of the fourteen-week ethics course, every lesson and its materials

sections.heading: Lessons that remember each other
sections.body: Lesson plans used to be written side by side, each knowing only the others’ titles, so one lesson could give a bean plant five stages and the next only four. Now each plan is written knowing what the lessons before it taught: the same terms and stages, the same cases, and anything still under way, like seeds sprouting by the window, carried on as it was set up. Each lesson lists only the vocabulary it introduces.

image.alt: Before: four lessons planned alone contradict each other. Now: each plan reads the ones before it

sections.heading: Plans you can teach as written
sections.body: Every plan now reads the way an experienced teacher would want it before walking into class.
bullets: Safety notes for anything students handle, taste, heat or cut, such as allergies or materials that must never be eaten.
Realistic timing for things that take days, counted against how often the class meets.
When a plan shows students how their work is scored, it uses the rubric’s own levels.
Slides shown during a test give its instructions only, never the answers.
Homework steps can be done at home, without a partner or classroom materials.
Other lessons are “last time” and “next time”, not quoted titles.

image.alt: A grade 2 lesson plan with key ideas, timed segments and teacher notes

sections.heading: Every material agrees with the plan
sections.body: Each plan gets a second read before anything is built on it. If the plan is written again, what that read found now goes into the rewrite, so the same mistake isn’t made twice. The reviewer also knows the slides, quiz and rubric are written separately, so it no longer asks for them inside the plan.

image.alt: Brief, outline, lesson plan, second read, and the materials written from the plan

sections.heading: Your files, cited by name
sections.body: When you attach articles or notes, Folio now refers to them by title or author, the way you would with students, never by internal passage numbers.

compare.before: The evidence is Torres’s report in passage [6] that students slept more.
compare.after: The evidence is Torres’s report that Seattle students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights.

sections.heading: Assessment that adds up
sections.body: When one graded piece is built across several lessons, each lesson now writes its own part, with its own title, instead of each claiming the whole grade. And when a course has weekly work as well as larger papers, every paper is set in a lesson, so none goes missing.

compare.before: Life cycle drawing and labeling check (“worth 100% of the course grade”) · Life cycle drawing and labeling check
compare.after: Life cycle drawing and labeling check: bean plant stage · Life cycle drawing and labeling check: butterfly and frog

sections.heading: How we find what to fix
sections.body: These improvements came from a new routine. We write real courses from teachers’ briefs, from grade 2 to university, check every part, and read each lesson as the teacher who would teach it. For every problem we ask why Folio wrote it and whether it would happen in another course. If it would, we fix the cause, so every teacher’s course gets better, not just the one we read.

image.alt: The quality routine: write real courses, check, read as a teacher, ask why, fix the cause, verify
